observatory.title: Observatory
observatory.description: A planet generated entirely in code: terrain, craters, clouds, rings and atmosphere, with no downloaded texture.
observatory.note: Everything is generated in code at load time: terrain, craters, clouds, rings and sky. No texture is downloaded.
observatory.hint: Drag to orbit · scroll to zoom

systems.title: Planetary systems
systems.description: The Solar System planet by planet, four real exoplanet systems, and systems generated on demand.
systems.generatedNote: Fictional but physically consistent: orbits follow Kepler's third law, temperatures follow the star's luminosity.
systems.scaleNote: Sizes, distances and speeds are compressed to fit the screen; the values shown are real.
systems.hintOrbit: Hover to identify · click to inspect · Space to pause
systems.hintCarousel: Scroll or ← → to browse · click or Enter to inspect
systems.hintInspect: Drag to rotate · scroll to zoom · Esc to go back
systems.starNote: Luminosity derived from radius and temperature (Stefan–Boltzmann law).
systems.generateHint: A new seed, a new system
systems.moonsLegend: Radius · distance from the planet · orbital period
systems.hintMoons: Click a moon to inspect it

credits.title: Credits
credits.description: Sources of the planetary maps and data.
credits.fontsNote: Instrument Serif, Geist and Geist Mono, via Google Fonts (SIL Open Font License).
credits.code: Everything else (procedural planets, atmospheres, rings, stars, sky, catalogue objects) is generated in code.
credits.objectsNote: Each object's figures come from the pages cited on its sheet (English Wikipedia, which links to the original publications). The nebulae, galaxies and black-hole simulations are generated in code; only Pluto and Ceres use a real map.
credits.modelsNote: International Space Station, Hubble, James Webb and Voyager 1: models from NASA 3D Resources (free of copyright), compressed for the web. Tiangong and Sputnik 1 are modelled in code.
credits.cometModelNote: Nucleus of comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko: NAVCAM shape model of November 2015, compressed for the web and redistributed under the same licence.
credits.starsNote: Positions, distances, magnitudes and spectra: HYG database v4.1 (astronexus, CC BY-SA 4.0), compiled from the Hipparcos, Gaia, Yale and Gliese catalogues; the site's star files derive from it and carry the same licence. Figure lines: d3-celestial by Olaf Frohn (BSD 3-Clause licence).

objects.title: Space objects
objects.description: Black holes, pulsars, quasars, galaxies, nebulae, comets, dwarf planets and spacecraft: real examples with their known data, modelled in 3D.
objects.hint: Drag to rotate · scroll to zoom

appearance.texture: Real surface map (NASA / USGS, public domain).
appearance.model: Built 3D model at real dimensions, generated textures.
appearance.simulation: Simulation: light paths and effects computed, colours and scales illustrative.
appearance.impression: Artist's view: shape and colours based on real images, procedural structure.
appearance.nasaModel: NASA's official 3D model (NASA 3D Resources, public domain).
appearance.shapeModel: Real shape of the nucleus: ESA's 3D model computed from Rosetta's images. Coma and tails: artist's view.
appearance.computedColour: Colour computed by the cited study from the star's spectrum; surface: artist's view.
appearance.textureFilled: Real New Horizons map (NASA, public domain). The southern hemisphere, in polar night during the 2015 flyby, was never imaged: it is filled in from the known terrain.
appearance.measuredShape: Nucleus built from its dimensions measured by Vega and Giotto in 1986; fine relief, coma and tails: artist's view.

black-holes.name: Black holes
black-holes.blurb: Regions where gravity holds back even light. They are only seen through what surrounds them: the matter falling in and heating up, and the background starlight they bend.

stars.name: Stars
stars.blurb: Stars with a surprising look. A white dwarf is not always white: when its very dense atmosphere holds planetary debris or carbon, it can look green, pink or blue.

neutron-stars.name: Neutron stars
neutron-stars.blurb: The collapsed cores of massive stars: more than a solar mass in a ball some twenty kilometres across. Pulsars sweep space with their beams like lighthouses.

quasars.name: Quasars
quasars.blurb: The most luminous galactic nuclei, powered by a supermassive black hole devouring gas. They outshine whole galaxies and light up the young Universe.

galaxies.name: Galaxies
galaxies.blurb: Systems of billions of stars, gas and dust. Spiral, elliptical or irregular, their shape tells their history.

nebulae.name: Nebulae
nebulae.blurb: Clouds of gas and dust: nurseries where stars are born, or the remains of those that die.

comets.name: Comets
comets.blurb: Lumps of ice and dust from the outer Solar System. Near the Sun they unfurl a coma and two tails.

dwarf-planets.name: Dwarf planets
dwarf-planets.blurb: Worlds massive enough to be round, but that have not cleared their orbit. Five are recognised by the International Astronomical Union.

spacecraft.name: Spacecraft
spacecraft.blurb: Objects humanity has sent into space: crewed stations, telescopes, probes.

creator.title: Create
creator.description: Pick a kind of object and tune its physics: it rebuilds live, with its computed figures. The page link keeps your settings.

intro.black-hole: The lighter a black hole, the hotter its disk: a stellar one glows in X-rays, a giant one stays orange. Spin brings the disk's inner edge closer and powers the jets.
intro.pulsar: The period sets how fast it spins and the magnetic field how fast it brakes: a fast, strongly magnetised pulsar loses energy quickly and stays young. Above 10¹⁴ gauss it is a magnetar.
intro.nebula: A nebula's colour comes from the emission lines of its elements: hydrogen glows red, ionised oxygen teal, sulfur deep red. Percentages are relative.
intro.star: On the main sequence, mass sets everything: temperature, size, brightness, lifetime. Fast rotation strengthens magnetic activity and covers the star in spots. White dwarfs can take the colour of the elements in their atmosphere.

creator.note: Simplified textbook relations (Shakura–Sunyaev disk, dipole spin-down, mass–luminosity relations): orders of magnitude, not observatory models. Disk and line colours mapped to the visible.

constellations.title: Constellations
constellations.description: The 88 official constellations. Seen from Earth their stars draw a figure; in space they are often unrelated to each other, at very different distances.
constellations.pageDescription: The constellation {name} seen from Earth, then in 3D, with the real distance of each of its stars.
constellations.depth: They look like neighbours, but the nearest is {near} light-years away and the farthest {far}: the figure only exists as seen from here.
constellations.skyNote: Earth's point of view. Size, brightness and colour follow each star's magnitude and temperature; the figure's stars stand out, those of the surrounding field stay discreet.
constellations.depthNote: Each star is at its real distance. The blue lines start from Earth (the blue dot): look along them and the figure comes back together.
constellations.skyHint: Click a star for its fact sheet
constellations.clickHint: Click a star, in the sky or in the list, to see its fact sheet.
constellations.dataNote: Distances from Hipparcos and Gaia parallaxes (HYG database): beyond a few hundred light-years the uncertainty can exceed 20%.

measure.title: Measure a distance
measure.unknown: Unknown distance for one of the two stars: their separation cannot be computed.
measure.illusion: In space they are about {r} times farther apart than they look in the sky.
measure.method: Computed from their celestial coordinates and distances from Earth (HYG catalogue), not from positions in the scene.
measure.howto: Click two stars, in the sky or in the list. A third click replaces the second, clicking a chosen star removes it, Escape clears everything.

constellations.computedNote: Values marked "computed": estimated from the catalogue (temperature from the colour, radius from luminosity and temperature, mass for main-sequence stars).
